title: Cordless Spin Scrubbers: A Look at Three Models for Easier Tub and Sink Cleaning
subtitle: How these battery-powered brushes work, what they cannot do, and what to check before you buy one.
excerpt: A cordless spin scrubber turns the brush for you, and one maker says its extendable handle lets you clean without bending or stretching. Here is what to look for, plus three models from one brand and their prices.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Cleaning the bathtub usually means kneeling on hard tile, leaning over the edge and working a brush in small circles. For many of us, the knees and back give out long before the grout comes clean. The same goes for shower walls and the corners of a deep sink.

A cordless spin scrubber takes over the circling. It is a rechargeable brush that spins on its own, so you guide it instead of scrubbing back and forth. Some models have an extendable handle, which may cut down on how far you have to bend.

Inside the body is a battery and a small motor that turns a brush head. The heads can be swapped. The models below list head types such as flat, pointed, sponge and scour, or simply a number of heads. Check each maker's page for which head it suggests for which job.

You will see a few technical terms. RPM means how many times the brush turns each minute, so a higher number spins faster. Torque is twisting strength, which helps the brush keep turning when you press it against a surface. IPX7 is a water-resistance rating that the makers list for these scrubbers. Read the maker's instructions to learn how the scrubber and its charger should be kept dry.

A spin scrubber also has limits. It is meant for surfaces such as tile, tubs and sinks, not as a replacement for a mop or vacuum on a whole floor. You still have to hold it and press it against the surface, and that takes some grip and wrist effort. If your hands are stiff or sore, hold one in a store first, or make sure you can return it.

items: Reach: if bending is the main problem, look for a model with an extendable handle, and check how long the handle gets. A short handheld model may mean more bending, as a general rule.
Weight and grip: the three pages we looked at did not show weight. Try holding one in person, or check the return policy before you buy.
Battery life: runtime figures come from the maker, and the Swift page lists none. The three pages also did not show charge time. More minutes generally means fewer stops to recharge.
Speeds: some models offer more than one speed. The Swift lists 220 RPM as gentle and 300 RPM for tougher stains.
Brush heads: see which heads come in the box. Replacement heads cost extra, and none of the three pages showed their prices, so ask before you buy.
Controls: look at the buttons and any display before you buy, and pick whatever feels easiest for you. A display is one more thing to learn.
Returns and warranty: the three pages did not show a warranty. Read the return and warranty terms before buying, especially if you are not sure your grip is up to it.
Setup help: ask a family member to charge it, attach the heads and walk through the controls with you the first time.

sections.content: All three scrubbers above come from one maker, HOTO, and we have not read independent reviews of them. Prices and specs are as the maker published them. Other brands make spin scrubbers too, so it is worth comparing handle length, battery life and return terms across brands before you choose. Note that the Wand page gives conflicting motor specs (250 RPM in one place, 400 RPM in another), so ask the seller which is right.

Follow the instructions that come with your scrubber, including how to charge it and clean it. As general advice, try it first on a small, out-of-sight spot, especially on painted, coated or older surfaces. Press lightly and let the spinning brush do the work.

Wet tile is slippery, so take your time and keep a towel handy. If kneeling is hard, ask a family member to help with the low spots. Keep the charger and any electrical parts away from standing water, and check the maker's guidance on drying.
"Adjust the reach to clean comfortably without bending or stretching." HOTO, on its Swift EasyCare product page

On its Wand product page, HOTO says: "We're currently offering both the previous and updated versions of the electric scrubber." The two versions differ in the small flat brush and the sisal brush. Before you pay, confirm which version you are buying so you know which brushes you will get.
sections.label: Before You Buy

sections.content: A spin scrubber will not make cleaning fun, but it may make it shorter and easier on the knees. Pick one that feels comfortable in your hand and can be returned if it does not suit you. Then let the brush do the circling.

products.name: HOTO Swift EasyCare Cordless Spin Scrubber
products.blurb: For people who want an extendable handle that detaches for storage. It has two speeds (220 and 300 RPM) and four brush heads, though the page does not list battery runtime.

products.name: HOTO Wand Cordless Spin Scrubber
products.blurb: A slim, anti-slip scrubber the maker describes as designed for one-handed kitchen cleaning. It has 12 magnetic brush heads and the maker claims up to 210 minutes of runtime; the page does not list handle length.

products.name: HOTO Flexi Cordless Spin Scrubber
products.blurb: For people who want to change the brush angle. It adjusts to five angles, has a smart display and eight brush heads, and the maker claims up to 110 minutes of runtime.
